angular.question: What is Angular?
angular.answer: Angular is a frontend framework. We use it to build single-page applications (SPAs) using HTML and TypeScript. It gives us everything we need — like data binding, routing, forms, HTTP calls — all in one package.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular is a TypeScript-based frontend framework used to build dynamic single-page applications with features like data binding, routing, and dependency injection.
angular.example: Suppose you want to build an online shopping website. Instead of reloading the whole page every time user clicks something, Angular loads only the required part. So the experience becomes very smooth, like using a mobile app.
steps: Install Node.js from nodejs.org
Open terminal and run: npm install -g @angular/cli
Create new project: ng new my-app
Go inside folder: cd my-app
Start the app: ng serve
Open browser and go to http://localhost:4200

angular.question: What are standalone components in Angular?
angular.answer: Standalone components are a new way of writing components where you don't need NgModule. The component itself is self-contained — it directly imports whatever it needs. This was introduced in Angular 14 and became the default from Angular 17. It makes the code much simpler and cleaner, less boilerplate.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Standalone components are self-contained Angular components that don’t require NgModules and manage their own dependencies using the imports array.
angular.example: For example, in a dashboard application, you can create a standalone component for a user profile that directly imports CommonModule and HttpClientModule. When this component loads, it can fetch user data from an API and display it without being declared in any NgModule, making development faster and reducing unnecessary module dependencies.
steps: Create a component with standalone: true in the @Component decorator
Import required modules directly in the imports array
No need to declare it in any NgModule
Use it directly in other standalone components or bootstrap it in main.ts

angular.question: What is dependency injection in Angular?
angular.answer: Dependency Injection (DI) means instead of a class creating its own dependencies, Angular provides them from outside. This makes code modular, easy to test, and easy to maintain.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Dependency Injection in Angular is a design pattern where dependencies are provided to a class from external sources instead of being created inside the class.
angular.example: For example, in a real application, a component may need to fetch user data from an API. Instead of directly creating an HTTP service inside the component, Angular injects a DataService into the constructor. This service can internally use HttpClient to call APIs. If you later replace the API or mock the service for testing, you only update the service without changing the component, improving maintainability and testability.

Write your business logic inside the service
In your component, add the service in the constructor
Angular will automatically create and inject the service instance
Use the service methods inside your component

angular.question: What are Angular signals?
angular.answer: Signals are a new reactive feature introduced in Angular 16. A signal is like a container that holds a value, and whenever the value changes, Angular automatically knows about it and updates the UI. No need for manual change detection. It is simpler and faster than Observables for many cases.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular signals are a reactive state management feature that automatically tracks and updates UI when the signal value changes without relying on change detection.
angular.example: For example, in a shopping cart component, you can use a signal to store the cart item count. Whenever a user adds or removes a product, the signal updates automatically, and the UI reflects the new count instantly. You can also use a computed signal to calculate the total price based on cart items, ensuring the UI stays in sync without manually subscribing or triggering change detection.

angular.question: What is the difference between ngOnInit and constructor?
angular.answer: Constructor is a TypeScript feature — it runs when the class is created. Use it only for simple things like injecting services. ngOnInit is an Angular lifecycle hook — it runs after Angular has set up the component's inputs and bindings. So for any logic that depends on @Input values or needs to call APIs, use ngOnInit.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Constructor is used for dependency injection and basic setup, while ngOnInit is an Angular lifecycle hook used for initialization logic after inputs are set.
angular.example: For example, in a parent-child component setup, a child component may receive a userId using @Input from the parent. This value is not available in the constructor, so calling an API using that userId inside the constructor will fail or give incorrect data. Instead, in ngOnInit, Angular ensures that @Input values are initialized, so you can safely call a service to fetch user details based on userId.
steps: Use constructor only for dependency injection
Implement OnInit interface in your component
Write your initialization logic inside ngOnInit()
Remember: @Input values are NOT available in constructor
@Input values ARE available in ngOnInit

angular.question: What is RxJS and how is it used in Angular?
angular.answer: RxJS stands for Reactive Extensions for JavaScript. It helps us handle asynchronous operations like API calls, user events, and timers using Observables. Angular uses RxJS heavily — especially in HttpClient, Reactive Forms, and Router. You can chain operators like map, filter, switchMap to transform data streams.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: RxJS is a library for handling asynchronous data using Observables, widely used in Angular for API calls, events, and reactive programming.
angular.example: For example, in a search feature, when a user types in an input box, you can use RxJS operators like debounceTime and switchMap to delay API calls and cancel previous requests. This prevents multiple unnecessary API calls and improves performance by only fetching the latest search result.

angular.question: What is Angular CLI?
angular.answer: Angular CLI (Command Line Interface) is a tool that helps us create, develop, and build Angular applications from the terminal. It generates boilerplate code, runs the dev server, creates production builds, and much more. It saves us a lot of time and keeps the project structure consistent.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular CLI is a command-line tool used to create, manage, and build Angular applications efficiently with predefined best practices.
angular.example: For example, in a real project, instead of manually creating folders, files, and configurations for a new component, you can run 'ng generate component user-profile'. Angular CLI automatically creates the component files, updates module or standalone imports, and follows best practices. Similarly, you can use 'ng serve' to run a local development server and 'ng build' to generate optimized production-ready files.

angular.question: Explain Angular lifecycle hooks
angular.answer: Lifecycle hooks are special methods that Angular calls at specific moments during a component's life. From the time the component is created to the time it is destroyed, Angular gives us hooks so we can run our own code at the right moment. The most commonly used ones are ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngOnDestroy, and ngAfterViewInit.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular lifecycle hooks are predefined methods that are called at different stages of a component’s lifecycle, allowing developers to execute logic at the right time.
angular.example: For example, in a user profile component, ngOnInit can be used to call an API and load user data when the component is initialized. If the component receives updated @Input data from a parent, ngOnChanges can react to those changes. ngAfterViewInit can be used to access DOM elements or child components after the view is fully rendered, and ngOnDestroy is used to clean up subscriptions or intervals to prevent memory leaks when the component is removed.

angular.question: What is two-way data binding?
angular.answer: Two-way data binding means the data flows in both directions — from component to template AND from template back to component. When you type something in an input field, the variable in the component updates automatically. And if the variable changes in the component, the input field shows the new value. In Angular, we use [(ngModel)] for this.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Two-way data binding in Angular allows automatic synchronization of data between the component and the template using [(ngModel)].
angular.example: For example, in a user profile form, you can bind an input field to a 'username' variable using [(ngModel)]. When the user types in the input, the component variable updates instantly. If you programmatically update the 'username' (e.g., after fetching data from an API), the input field automatically reflects the new value, keeping both UI and component state in sync.

angular.question: What is lazy loading in Angular?
angular.answer: Lazy loading means loading parts of your application only when the user actually needs them, not at the start. This reduces the initial bundle size, so the app loads faster. When user navigates to a particular route, only then that module or component is downloaded. Very useful for big enterprise applications.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Lazy loading in Angular is a technique to load feature modules or components only when a specific route is accessed, improving initial load performance.
angular.example: For example, in a large enterprise application, modules like 'Admin', 'Reports', or 'Settings' are not required on initial load. Using lazy loading, these features are loaded only when the user navigates to their respective routes. This reduces the initial bundle size, speeds up application startup, and improves overall performance, especially for users on slow networks.

angular.question: What are Angular pipes?
angular.answer: Pipes are simple functions that transform data in the template before displaying it. Angular has built-in pipes like DatePipe, UpperCasePipe, CurrencyPipe, and AsyncPipe. You can also create your own custom pipes. You use them with the | (pipe) symbol in your template.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular pipes are used to transform and format data in templates using the pipe (|) operator.
angular.example: For example, in a user dashboard, you may receive raw data from an API like timestamps, names, or prices. You can use built-in pipes like date to format timestamps, uppercase to format names, and currency to display prices properly. If you are using an Observable for API data, the async pipe automatically subscribes and updates the UI when data arrives, removing the need for manual subscription handling.

angular.question: What is change detection in Angular?
angular.answer: Change detection is how Angular keeps the view (HTML) in sync with the component data. Whenever something happens — like a button click, API response, or timer — Angular checks all the components to see if any data changed, and updates the DOM accordingly. It uses Zone.js to detect async operations automatically.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Change detection in Angular is the process of updating the DOM when component data changes.
angular.example: For example, in a dashboard component, when an API call returns new data (like updated user stats), Angular automatically detects the change and updates the UI without manual DOM manipulation. With Default strategy, Angular checks all components, but with OnPush, it only updates when input references change or events occur, improving performance in large applications.

angular.question: What are Angular directives?
angular.answer: Directives are special instructions that tell Angular to do something with a DOM element. There are three types — Component directives (components themselves), Structural directives (like *ngIf, *ngFor, @if, @for that add/remove elements from DOM), and Attribute directives (like ngClass, ngStyle that change appearance or behavior).
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular directives are classes that modify the structure or behavior of DOM elements.
angular.example: For example, in a user dashboard, you can use a structural directive like @if to show or hide sections based on user login status. You can use @for to dynamically render a list of items from API data. Additionally, an attribute directive like ngClass can apply different styles based on conditions, such as highlighting active users. Custom directives can also be created to add reusable behaviors like highlighting elements or handling permissions.

angular.question: What is Angular routing?
angular.answer: Routing in Angular allows you to navigate between different views (pages) without reloading the browser. You define URL paths and map them to components. Angular Router supports features like route parameters, guards for security, lazy loading, and child routes for nested layouts.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular routing is used to navigate between components based on URL paths without reloading the page.
angular.example: For example, in an e-commerce application, you can define routes like '/products' to show a product list and '/product/101' to show details of a specific product using route parameters. Angular Router dynamically loads the corresponding component into the router-outlet without refreshing the page. You can also use route guards to restrict access to certain routes like '/checkout' unless the user is authenticated.

angular.question: What are template-driven forms vs reactive forms?
angular.answer: Template-driven forms are simple — you write most logic in the HTML using ngModel. They are good for basic forms. Reactive forms are more powerful — you define the form structure in the TypeScript class using FormGroup and FormControl. Reactive forms give you more control, are easier to test, and are better for complex forms with dynamic validation.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Template-driven forms rely on template logic using ngModel, while reactive forms define form structure and validation in the component using FormGroup and FormControl.
angular.example: For example, in a login form, a template-driven approach is suitable for simple input fields with basic validation. However, in a complex registration form with dynamic fields (like adding multiple phone numbers), conditional validation, and real-time validation feedback, reactive forms are preferred because you can programmatically control form state, add/remove controls dynamically, and write unit tests more easily.

angular.question: What is Angular HttpClient?
angular.answer: HttpClient is Angular's built-in service for making HTTP requests to APIs. It returns Observables, supports typed responses, and has features like interceptors for modifying requests and error handling. In standalone apps, you enable it with provideHttpClient() in your app config.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular HttpClient is a service used to make HTTP requests and handle API communication using Observables.
angular.example: For example, in a user management system, you can use HttpClient to fetch a list of users from an API when the component loads, send new user data using POST when a form is submitted, and delete a user using DELETE. You can also use interceptors to automatically attach authentication tokens to every request and handle errors globally, making API communication clean and maintainable.

angular.question: What are Angular interceptors?
angular.answer: Interceptors are like middlemen that sit between your app and the server. Every HTTP request goes through them before reaching the server, and every response passes through them before reaching your code. You can use them to add auth tokens, log requests, show loaders, or handle errors globally.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Angular interceptors are functions that intercept HTTP requests and responses to modify or handle them globally.
angular.example: For example, in a secured application, you can use an interceptor to automatically attach a JWT token to every outgoing API request instead of manually adding it in each service call. You can also use another interceptor to handle API errors globally (like redirecting to login on 401 errors) or to show and hide a loading spinner during API calls, ensuring consistent behavior across the entire app.

angular.question: What is NgRx?
angular.answer: NgRx is a state management library for Angular, inspired by Redux. It helps manage application state in one central place called the Store. It uses Actions to describe events, Reducers to update state, Effects for side effects like API calls, and Selectors to read state. Very useful for large, complex applications.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: NgRx is a state management library for Angular that uses a centralized store with actions, reducers, effects, and selectors to manage application state.
angular.example: For example, in an e-commerce application, when a user clicks 'Load Products', an action is dispatched. An effect listens to this action, calls an API to fetch products, and then dispatches a success action with the data. The reducer updates the store with the new product list, and components use selectors to automatically get the updated data. This ensures predictable state management and makes debugging easier in large applications.

angular.question: What is ViewChild and ContentChild?
angular.answer: ViewChild lets you access a child component, directive, or DOM element that is inside your component's own template. ContentChild lets you access projected content — content that a parent passes between your component's tags using <ng-content>. Both are available after specific lifecycle hooks.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: ViewChild accesses elements or components from the component’s own template, while ContentChild accesses projected content passed from a parent component.
angular.example: For example, using ViewChild, you can access an input field inside your component and set focus after the view initializes. Using ContentChild, if your component uses <ng-content> to accept content from a parent (like a custom card component), you can access and manipulate that projected content, such as reading a directive applied by the parent. ViewChild works with internal template elements, while ContentChild works with external projected content.

angular.question: What is the purpose of Angular guards?
angular.answer: Route guards control who can access which route. They act like security checkpoints. CanActivate checks if a user can open a route. CanDeactivate checks if user can leave a route. Resolve pre-fetches data before the route loads. In modern Angular, guards can be simple functions.

If the user is not logged in, the guard redirects them to the login page. You can also use a Resolve guard to fetch user profile data before the route loads, ensuring the component has all required data when it initializes. This improves security and user experience.

angular.question: What is TypeScript?
angular.answer: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript made by Microsoft. It adds static typing, interfaces, enums, generics, and decorators on top of JavaScript. Angular is built entirely with TypeScript. The big advantage is that errors are caught at compile time, not at runtime, so code becomes more reliable and easier to maintain.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: TypeScript is a strongly typed superset of JavaScript that adds static typing and advanced features to improve code quality and maintainability.
angular.example: For example, in an Angular application, when you define a User interface and use it in a service or component, TypeScript ensures that the API response matches the expected structure. If a required field is missing or has the wrong type, TypeScript throws an error during development, preventing runtime bugs and making the code more predictable and easier to debug.

angular.question: What is the difference between Observable and Promise?
angular.answer: Promise handles a single async value and executes immediately (eager). Observable handles multiple values over time and executes only when you subscribe (lazy). Observables can be cancelled, support operators for transformation, and are the backbone of Angular's HTTP and reactive patterns.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Promise handles a single async value and executes immediately, while Observable handles multiple values over time and starts execution on subscription.
angular.example: For example, when making an HTTP API call in Angular, HttpClient returns an Observable because it allows you to use operators like map, switchMap, and retry, and also cancel the request if needed. In contrast, a Promise is useful for one-time operations like fetching a configuration file, but it cannot be cancelled or handle multiple values like an Observable stream (e.g., real-time data or user events).

angular.question: What is AOT compilation?
angular.answer: AOT (Ahead-of-Time) compilation converts your Angular templates and TypeScript into optimized JavaScript during the build process, before the browser downloads the app. This means faster rendering, smaller bundles, early error detection, and better security. AOT is the default for production builds in Angular.

angular.example: For example, in a production Angular application, when you run 'ng build --configuration production', Angular compiles all templates and components into efficient JavaScript before deployment. This removes the need for the Angular compiler in the browser, reduces bundle size, and catches template errors (like misspelled variables) during build time instead of at runtime, resulting in faster load times and more reliable applications.

angular.question: What is the difference between let, const, and var?
angular.answer: var has function scope and gets hoisted — it can cause unexpected bugs. let has block scope and can be reassigned. const also has block scope but cannot be reassigned (though objects and arrays it holds can still be modified internally). In modern TypeScript/JavaScript, use const by default, let when you need to reassign, and avoid var completely.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: var is function-scoped and hoisted, let is block-scoped and reassignable, and const is block-scoped but cannot be reassigned.
angular.example: For example, in an Angular component, if you use var inside a loop or condition, it can leak outside its block and cause unexpected behavior. Using let ensures the variable is limited to the block scope, avoiding bugs. const is best for values like configuration, API URLs, or injected services that should not be reassigned, improving code safety and readability.

angular.question: What are decorators in Angular?
angular.answer: Decorators are special functions that add metadata (extra information) to classes, methods, or properties. angular.question: What is content projection in Angular?
angular.answer: Content projection allows you to pass HTML content from a parent component into a child component's template. angular.question: What is Zone.js?
angular.answer: Zone.js is a library that patches all browser async APIs (setTimeout, Promises, event listeners, etc.) so Angular can know when an async operation completes. This is how Angular's automatic change detection works — Zone.js tells Angular 'something happened, check for changes now.' Angular 17+ is experimenting with going zoneless using signals.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Zone.js is a library that tracks asynchronous operations and triggers Angular’s change detection automatically.
angular.example: For example, when an HTTP request completes or a button click event occurs, Zone.js intercepts these async operations and notifies Angular to run change detection and update the UI. In performance-critical scenarios like heavy computations or animations, you can run code outside Angular’s zone using NgZone.runOutsideAngular() to avoid unnecessary change detection cycles, and re-enter using NgZone.run() when UI updates are needed.

angular.question: What is tree shaking?
angular.answer: Tree shaking is a build optimization technique that removes unused code from the final JavaScript bundle. The bundler analyzes which functions, classes, and modules are actually imported and used, and removes everything else. This makes your app smaller and faster to load. angular.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
angular.answer: Authentication means verifying WHO you are — like showing your Aadhaar card at the bank to prove your identity. Authorization means checking WHAT you are allowed to do — like the bank checking whether you have permission to access a particular locker. In Angular apps, authentication checks if the user is logged in (valid credentials), and authorization checks if the logged-in user has the right role or permission to access a page or feature.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Authentication verifies user identity, while authorization determines what actions or resources the user is allowed to access.
angular.example: For example, in an Angular application, when a user logs in, the app sends credentials to the backend and receives a JWT token (authentication). This token is stored and attached to future API requests using an HTTP interceptor. Then, when the user tries to access routes like '/admin', a route guard checks the user's role (authorization) and allows or restricts access based on permissions.

angular.question: What is a Reducer in NgRx?
angular.answer: A Reducer is a pure function in NgRx that takes the current state and an action, and returns a new state. It never modifies the existing state — it always creates a new copy. angular.question: How do Actions, Reducers, Effects, and Selectors work together in NgRx?

angular.question: What is the Redux pattern and why use it with Angular?

angular.question: What are Smart (Container) and Dumb (Presentational) Components?
angular.answer: Smart and Dumb component pattern is a design approach to keep your Angular code clean and maintainable. Smart Components (also called Container Components) handle the business logic — they talk to services, manage state, make API calls, and pass data down to child components. Dumb Components (also called Presentational Components) only receive data through @Input() and send events back through @Output(). They don't know where the data comes from — they just display it. This separation keeps UI reusable and business logic centralized.

angular.question: What are Observables in Angular and how do they work?

angular.question: What are switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, and forkJoin? When to use which?
angular.answer: These are higher-order mapping operators in RxJS — they map each emitted value to a new inner Observable. switchMap cancels the previous inner Observable when a new value arrives — best for search/typeahead where only the latest result matters. mergeMap runs all inner Observables concurrently — best when you want parallel execution and all results. concatMap queues inner Observables and runs them one after another — best when order matters. forkJoin waits for multiple Observables to complete and emits all final values together — best for parallel API calls where you need all results at once (like Promise.all).

In a dashboard, forkJoin is used to fetch users, orders, and stats APIs together and render the UI only after all responses arrive.

angular.question: What is Lazy Loading in Angular and how to implement it?

Without lazy loading, Angular bundles everything into one file, and the user has to download the entire app even if they only visit one page. With lazy loading, each feature is in a separate chunk that downloads on demand. In Angular 17 with standalone components, you can lazy load individual components directly in the route configuration using loadComponent, or lazy load a group of child routes using loadChildren.

angular.question: What are Retry and Caching Strategies for HTTP calls in Angular?
angular.answer: In real-world apps, API calls can fail due to network issues, server overloads, or timeouts. Retry strategies automatically re-attempt failed requests. Caching strategies store API responses so you don't make the same request again. RxJS provides retry() and retryWhen() operators for retries. For caching, you can use shareReplay() to cache the Observable result, or build a custom caching interceptor. Angular's HttpClient also supports HTTP caching headers (ETag, Cache-Control). Best practices: 1) Only retry on transient errors (5xx, timeout), not client errors (4xx). 2) Use exponential backoff — wait longer between each retry. 3) Cache GET requests only, never cache POST/PUT/DELETE. 4) Set cache TTL (time-to-live) so stale data gets refreshed.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: Retry strategies reattempt failed HTTP calls, while caching avoids duplicate requests by storing responses, improving performance and reliability.
angular.example: For example, in a product listing page, if the API fails due to a temporary server issue, the app retries the request with exponential backoff before showing an error. Once the data is successfully fetched, it is cached using shareReplay or an HTTP interceptor. If the user revisits the page within a short time, the cached data is served instantly without another API call, improving performance and reducing server load.

angular.question: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) in Angular and when to use it?
angular.answer: Server-Side Rendering means the Angular app is rendered on the server first, and the fully-formed HTML is sent to the browser. Without SSR (Client-Side Rendering), the browser gets an empty HTML shell and has to download, parse, and execute JavaScript before showing content. With SSR, users see content instantly, and search engines can crawl the page properly. Angular uses Angular Universal (now built-in as @angular/ssr in Angular 17) for SSR. There are two modes: 1) Full SSR — server renders every request dynamically. 2) Static Site Generation (SSG/Prerendering) — pages are rendered at build time. SSR is best for content-heavy, SEO-critical, public-facing apps. For internal dashboards or admin panels, CSR is usually fine.
angular.interviewBestShortAnswer: SSR renders Angular apps on the server and sends ready HTML to the browser, improving SEO and initial load performance.
angular.example: For example, in an e-commerce website, product listing and detail pages are rendered on the server so users and search engines can see content instantly. When the page loads in the browser, Angular hydrates it and makes it interactive. This improves SEO rankings and reduces Time to First Contentful Paint (FCP), especially for slow networks or mobile devices.

angular.question: What is Module Federation and Micro Frontend architecture in Angular?

angular.question: What are the different State Management approaches in Angular?
angular.answer: State management is about how you store, update, and share data across components in your Angular app. There are several approaches depending on app complexity: 1) Component State — simple @Input/@Output for parent-child communication. 2) Services with Signals/BehaviorSubject — medium complexity, shared service acts as a store. 3) NgRx (Redux pattern) — for large, complex apps with predictable state flow (Actions → Reducers → Store → Selectors). 4) NgRx ComponentStore — lightweight alternative for component-scoped state. 5) NGXS — simpler Redux-like library with less boilerplate. 6) Akita — entity-based state management. For most apps, Services with Signals is enough. Use NgRx only when state is complex, shared across many components, or needs time-travel debugging.

This ensures predictable state changes and easier debugging.

angular.question: What is Angular Application Architecture and how to design it properly?
angular.answer: Angular application architecture is the overall structure and patterns you follow to build a maintainable, scalable, and testable app. A well-architected Angular app follows these layers: 1) Presentation Layer — smart and dumb components that handle the UI. 2) Business Logic Layer — services that contain the app's rules and workflows. 3) Data Access Layer — services that communicate with APIs, localStorage, or databases. 4) State Management Layer — manages shared data across the app. 5) Routing Layer — controls navigation and lazy loading. The principles are: Separation of Concerns (each layer does one thing), Single Responsibility (each class has one job), DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), and SOLID principles. unitTest.question: What is Karma and Jasmine in Angular testing? How do they work together?

unitTest.question: How to mock dependencies and spy on methods in Jasmine and Jest?
unitTest.answer: Mocking is the technique of replacing real dependencies with fake ones during testing. This ensures you test only the unit under test, not its dependencies. In Jasmine, you use jasmine.createSpyObj() to create mock objects with spy methods, and spyOn() to spy on existing methods. In Jest, you use jest.fn() for mock functions, jest.spyOn() for spying, and jest.mock() for mocking entire modules. Both frameworks let you control what the mock returns (returnValue), track how many times it was called (toHaveBeenCalled), and verify call arguments (toHaveBeenCalledWith). The key rule: mock everything external (services, HTTP, router, localStorage) and test only the logic of the unit.

You control its return values and verify whether methods like login() were called with correct arguments — without hitting real APIs.

unitTest.question: How to test Async code, Observables, and Promises in Angular tests?
unitTest.answer: Angular apps are full of async operations — HTTP calls, timers, Promises, Observables. Testing async code requires special handling. unitTest.question: What is Code Coverage in Angular testing and how to generate reports?
unitTest.answer: Code coverage measures how much of your source code is actually executed by your tests. It reports four metrics: 1) Statements — percentage of code statements executed. 2) Branches — percentage of if/else, switch, ternary paths tested. 3) Functions — percentage of functions called during tests. 4) Lines — percentage of code lines covered. In Angular with Karma, you run 'ng test --code-coverage' and it generates an HTML report using Istanbul/nyc. With Jest, you run 'npx jest --coverage'. Industry standard is 80%+ coverage, but 100% is not always practical or necessary. Focus on testing critical business logic, happy paths, and error handling rather than chasing 100% on every file.
